title: Tenali Raman and the Scholar of Kalinga
summary: A formidable scholar from Kalinga named Mahadeva Shastri arrived at the court of Vijayanagara. He was a master of palindromic poetry (*Gatagata-kavya*)—verses that read identica...
full_text:
A formidable scholar from Kalinga named Mahadeva Shastri arrived at the court of Vijayanagara. He was a master of palindromic poetry (*Gatagata-kavya*)—verses that read identically forward and backward, letter for letter, retaining poetic meter and philosophical meaning.
He challenged the court:
'Let any poet of Vijayanagara compose an eight-line classical verse praising the Emperor that reads identically forward and backward! If none can match me before noon, your court must surrender its poetic laurels!'

The royal poets struggled for hours. Crafting a single rhyming line forward and backward without creating gibberish was excruciatingly difficult.
King Krishnadevaraya looked anxiously at Tenali Raman.

Tenali stepped forward with a smile:
'Maharaj, composing verses that read forward and backward is child’s play in Vijayanagara.
In fact, my very name is a divine palindrome!'

The scholar frowned: 'Thy name?'
Tenali declared:
'Indeed! In our Telugu language, my name is written:
**VI - KA - TA - KA - VI** (The Jester-Poet)!
Read it forward: *VI-KA-TA-KA-VI*!
Read it backward: *VI-KA-TA-KA-VI*!
My name was born an eternal palindrome, before I ever wrote a single line of verse!'

Tenali then picked up an iron stylus and engraved an eight-line masterpiece upon a palm leaf.
The verse praised King Krishnadevaraya’s valor in war and benevolence in peace.
When read forward, it was a soaring hymn of royal victory;
When read backward, letter for letter, it formed an equally sublime hymn praising the King’s compassion and justice!

The scholar from Kalinga read the palm leaf forward, then backward, checking every syllable with trembling fingers.
He could not find a single flaw in meter, grammar, or sentiment.

The scholar bowed low, laid his gold-embroidered shawl at Tenali’s feet, and confessed:
'Tenali Raman, thou art truly *Vikatakavi*—a poet whose mind moves in all directions with peerless grace!'
King Krishnadevaraya rewarded Tenali with a chest of pearls, celebrating that true mastery wears its genius with lightness and joy.
moral: Intellectual vanity that seeks to defeat others through linguistic acrobatics is disarmed by simple wit.
